messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus Chen

Marcus Chen, forty-six, sits with his hands folded so tightly his knuckles have gone white. He is a firefighter in Sacramento, a man built for crisis and trained to act, yet he speaks in a voice stripped of its usual authority. The trauma that brought him to this office began not in the streets he patrols but in a conflict zone half a world away, eight years ago, when he took a leave of absence to work as a relief worker in a war-torn region of Southeast Asia. What he encountered there has never left him.

During his third month, Marcus and two colleagues were assessing a damaged medical facility when a mortar round struck nearby. The explosion came without warning—a sound that seemed to rupture the air itself and fling him sideways into rubble. When the dust cleared, he found himself alive but his colleague Sorn, a young Cambodian interpreter, was not. The worst part came after: in the chaos of evacuation, Marcus witnessed the clinic's director—a man he had come to trust—taking supplies meant for patients and selling them to armed groups. The moral machinery that had held Marcus together fractured in that moment. He had come to save lives, and he had failed. He had worked alongside corruption. He had survived when Sorn had not.

He returned to the States and tried to resume his life as a firefighter. For the first year, he managed. But then, on a routine call in 2019, a car backfired near the station. The sharp bang catapulted him back to that moment—his chest seized, his hands trembled, and suddenly he was certain something catastrophic was about to happen. The memory didn't return as a coherent narrative; instead it came in fragments that wouldn't arrange themselves in order. He could see Sorn's face, then the director's hands, then the rubble, but the sequence made no sense. He knew what had happened, but when he tried to explain it to his captain, the words dissolved. All he could say was: "I was there. Something bad happened." The inability to articulate it only deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally broken.

Any unexpected noise now—a car door slamming, a motorcycle engine, even the sound of voices raised in argument—sent him spiraling. When someone mentioned in the station's break room that they'd seen news coverage of sexual violence in conflict zones, Marcus felt a hot surge of shame and rage that he couldn't name. He had seen things. Things he couldn't protect people from. Things that had happened while he stood by. These triggers didn't just remind him of the trauma; they made him feel that he had acted in ways that went against everything he believed himself to be. He was supposed to be a protector. Instead, he had been complicit in a system of theft and suffering. His life, as he had understood it, was destroyed.

The weight of these convictions—that he was morally ruined, that he belonged nowhere—began to drive everything he did. He started performing small rituals, counting breaths in specific patterns, trying to mentally prevent the next disaster. When that didn't work, when the memories returned unbidden and he felt the phantom pain in his shoulders and ribs where the blast had thrown him, he would hurt himself deliberately—gripping his forearm until it bruised, pressing his fingernails into his palms—anything to replace the overwhelming dread with something he could control and understand. He would try desperately not to think about what happened, pushing the memories away with such force that he'd end up exhausted, only to have them crash through his defenses hours later with renewed intensity. The self-harm would follow, and then the rituals, a cycle that seemed to intensify the very memories he was trying to escape.

His threat system had become hypervigilant in a way that made no sense in his ordinary life. He was irritable with his colleagues, snapping at minor infractions. Unusual silence—a quiet station at night, a pause in conversation—made him certain something dangerous was imminent. The negative emotions came in waves: fear that he would hurt someone, horror at what he had witnessed, anger at the director and at himself, shame that he had survived. These feelings seemed to confirm what he already believed: that he was damaged beyond repair, that he no longer belonged in the brotherhood of firefighters, that his presence was a threat to others.

It was his ex-wife who finally insisted he seek help. She had noticed the bruises, the way he flinched at sounds, the emotional distance that had calcified into something like contempt for himself. Marcus came to this appointment because he was running out of places to hide, and because some small part of him—the part that still remembered why he had gone to that war zone in the first place—wondered if there was any way back from what he had become.
